title: Legendary photographer on getting that perfect election night picture
description:
Courtney Dorning

On election night, photographers will be in position, ready to snap history-making moments. It's something Pulitzer-prize-winner photographer David Hume Kennerly, has done for decades.

MARY LOUISE KELLY, HOST: This is ALL THINGS CONSIDERED from NPR News. I'm Mary Louise Kelly.SCOTT DETROW, HOST: And I'm Scott Detrow. Tonight, all over the country, candidates will be gathering with their supporters, their families and their staffs to see whether they won or lost. When those results come in, there will be joy, there will be sadness, there will be shock, there will be disappointment. And all of those human responses to the results, well, they can make great photographs. Tonight, photographers will also be in position ready to snap these history-making moments.That is something Pulitzer Prize-winning photographer David Hume Kennerly has done for much of the past six decades. And many of those election nights, as well as a whole lot else, are collected in Kennerly's new book, "In The Room: 60 Years On The Front Lines Of History." Kennerly covered Vietnam. He covered Ali v. Frazier. He also covered the 2000 presidential campaign between Texas Governor George W. Bush and Vice President Al Gore.And I want to talk about one particular moment. Bush has thought he's won this election. Al Gore has called him to concede. You take several pictures of him preparing his victory speech. And then, suddenly, Al Gore calls. He retracts the concession. Tell me what happens next.DAVID HUME KENNERLY: (Laughter) This is - you're describing what makes for really good pictures in my world. I will back it up a little bit from there. I had come over with Dick Cheney, and I'd covered the last, I think, week or two of the campaign with Cheney. So we went over to the governor's mansion when it looks like he was going to win, or they declared him the winner, and everything was great. There were a couple other photographers in there. And he got the phone call from Gore, but he took it upstairs. So he left. I didn't see him do that. But I went into the kitchen to get a drink of water, and Bush came down the back stairway and said - looked at me. He looked kind of shell-shocked, and he said, he took it back. He took it back. I said, who took what back? And he said, Gore just called me and took back his concession. And I went, well, that sucks. I didn't know what else to say.DETROW: (Laughter).KENNERLY: And so he went into that other small room, and you have this tableau of the Bush dynasty, former President Bush 41. You had Jeb Bush, who's the governor of Florida, and George W., who's the governor of Texas and thought he won the election. And so that picture caught it all. And if you look closely at it, which you can see it in the room, you see Mrs. Bush's hand is kind of crushed into her palm and the tension is palpable...DETROW: Yeah.KENNERLY: ...In the room. And you've got Cheney's there, and Don Evans, who was the campaign chairman.DETROW: You described it pretty well. But to me, here's the tension of the picture. George W. Bush is sitting in a chair in the center. He's kind of hunched a little bit over with his elbows on his knees, looking forward in thought. And then his brother Jeb is standing above him. He's the governor of Florida at the time. This is all his problem. And he looks incredibly tense. And then, off in the background, you have the former President George H.W. Bush making phone calls. So there's a lot emotionally going on here.KENNERLY: Well, there was one other element to that. So Jeb had been celebrating with having a drink or two. And you can see in that picture he looks concerned, at least, but he was totally sobered up at that point. He thought they'd won, and now they might lose. That was probably - I think probably my best political photograph.DETROW: What do you think a photograph tells us that video doesn't? I mean, we consume politics these days through social media, through reels, through short video clips, you know? But there's so much emotion that comes through in a still picture, and I think it's different. How do you think about that?KENNERLY: Well, for one thing, you're never going to see video in the room when it happened because video, then you would need sound with it, and conversations are being recorded. Photographers are incredibly discreet, and we - our currency is trust. So what you're seeing in still photos is the real picture of what's going on. You'll never see a video clip of that ever.DETROW: How do you think about positioning? Is it just instinctual at this point? Because you're clearly - you're in the room. You're trying to make people comfortable in the room. You're trying to get the right shot and be in the right place. How do you think about kind of your own movements as you're scanning and looking for the moments to capture?KENNERLY: Oh, that's a good question, and it's instinctive in my case. I remember when I first started with President Ford, the first three or four days, every time somebody would come into the Oval Office. He would say, oh, Senator Goldwater, meet David Kennerly, my photographer. And I had to train him. I said, please don't do that. I'm, like, missing pictures here. So pretty soon, I ended up being invisible, literally. And that's the trick. I mean, you can't teach that in school. Back to the Bush photo, that's a great example of it. They're so concentrated on watching this little TV about what's going on, no one was paying any attention to me. You can see that. I mean, that is a picture, like, taken by the invisible man, essentially.DETROW: You said at the beginning of the conversation that you thought that election night 2000 picture is your best political photograph. Do you have a favorite beyond that?KENNERLY: Well, yeah, I do, actually. And it's political, and it features George W. Bush. And it was at the African American Museum opening. And Michelle Obama, the first lady, came over to Bush before they started the ceremony and gave him a hug. And I nailed that picture. That one is a really important shot, particularly in the light of what's going on today where everybody throws rocks at each other. And here you have an African American woman, a white guy, a Republican, a Democrat, in this fantastic moment that was genuine. And I think that's sort of a fairy-tale picture in a way. We long for the days when politicians got along. And I - in the book, you'll see, I have a lot of examples of that. George Herbert Walker Bush as VP with Tip O'Neill yucking it up. John Kerry and John McCain, Democrat, Republican, Vietnam vets.DETROW: Going back to that 2016 image, I'm looking at it. And this - like, this really did kind of change both of their public images in terms of I feel like from that point forward, when they were on stage together, everyone was looking at them to see how they'd interact. They both look so comfortable. And his eyes are closed, and he's almost nuzzling into Michelle Obama, and it's just the sign of closeness. It's remarkable.KENNERLY: Well, it's also an example of where the picture doesn't tell the entire story, although that was a genuine moment, and I nailed that. However, when I give talks, I show the film clip of that happening. The picture conveyed a little more warm and fuzzier than it was. But it's an honest picture, however. I think that was the important thing.DETROW: Yeah. That's David Hume Kennerly. His new book is "In The Room: 60 Years On The Front Lines Of History." Thanks so much for talking to us.KENNERLY: Thank you.(SOUNDBITE OF CHARLI XCX SONG, "360") Copyright © 2026 NPR. All rights reserved.
